analysis.one_liner: Improves safety, break, and anti-retaliation rules for meat and poultry plant workers and restricts meatpackers' market practices.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote; it sat in five House committees until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required stricter oversight of line speeds in meat and poultry plants, limited attendance-point policies that punish workers for legally protected absences, added new OSHA safety standards (ergonomics, infectious disease, bathroom access), funded more OSHA inspectors, and given workers the right to sue employers who retaliate against them. It also would have restored country-of-origin labeling for beef, pork, and dairy, added $100 million for small meat processors, and restricted big meatpackers' contract and livestock-ownership practices. It was referred to five committees, sent to an Agriculture subcommittee, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Meat and poultry processing workers — several hundred thousand people, many of them immigrants and workers of color — would gain stronger protections from injuries at fast line speeds, guaranteed toilet-break access, retaliation protections with a private right to sue, and protections against attendance-point discipline for legally protected leave. Livestock ranchers and contract poultry growers would gain new remedies against packers and live poultry dealers under the Packers and Stockyards Act. Consumers would gain country-of-origin labels on beef, pork, and dairy. Small and regional meat processors would gain expanded grant funding.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits line-speed increases and waiver approvals unless a certified inspection shows no adverse impact on worker safety, and bars USDA funds from being used to raise line speeds during the covered period.

Restricts employers' use of no-fault attendance point policies unless they are disclosed in writing and do not penalize legally protected leave, with enforcement through FMLA-style remedies and civil penalties.

Directs OSHA to issue standards on ergonomics and infectious-disease exposure (including an emergency COVID-19 standard within 7 days), verify bathroom access, run a permanent regional emphasis inspection program for amputation, line-speed, chemical, and heat/cold hazards, and add a worker-designated representative on inspections.

Expands retaliation protections for meat and poultry workers, including a private right of action with compensatory and punitive damages, a presumption of retaliation for adverse actions within 90 days of protected activity, and a ban on waiver by arbitration or collective bargaining agreements.
Appropriates $60 million per year for fiscal years 2024 through 2029 to hire additional OSHA inspectors.

Restores mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef and pork and adds dairy products; expands meat and poultry processing grants ($100 million for FY2024-2033) with labor-peace-agreement conditions and restrictions on selling plants to large packers.

Adds unlawful practices under the Packers and Stockyards Act, restricting certain forward contracts, packer ownership and feeding of livestock beyond narrow exceptions, and conduct that adversely affects competition, plus new remedies for contract growers.

analysis.who_pays: Large meat and poultry processing companies would bear the cost: slower or restricted line speeds, new OSHA standards and inspections, attendance-policy compliance, retaliation lawsuits, and new limits on packer livestock ownership and contracts. Grocery retailers would bear labeling-compliance costs for country-of-origin labels. Federal spending on OSHA inspectors and processing grants would be financed by the Treasury.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes substantial compliance and operational costs on meat processors, including limits on line speeds and contract structures that packers argue reduce plant efficiency and throughput.
It appropriates roughly $360 million over six years for OSHA inspectors plus $100 million in processing grants without an offset, adding to federal spending.

The bill would supersede some poultry-tournament pay systems and restrict certain forward contracts, which packers and some contract growers contend provide flexibility and financing that benefit producers as well.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers covered, the safety gains — fewer musculoskeletal injuries and amputations, guaranteed bathroom access, and real retaliation remedies with a right to sue — outweigh the costs, which fall mainly on a small number of large, profitable packers and on federal spending. The COVID-era provisions arrive after the emergency they respond to, which limits their practical value. The main design question is whether the Packers and Stockyards restrictions on contracts and packer ownership help or complicate livestock markets; the bill nonetheless gives producers clearer legal remedies.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to five House committees in February 2023 and referred to an Agriculture subcommittee the next month, and no committee ever acted on it before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the bill on February 2, 2023, with five original cosponsors.

It was referred to the Committees on Agriculture, Education and the Workforce, Oversight and Accountability, House Administration, and Judiciary — a five-committee referral that requires any action to be coordinated across committees.
On March 2, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry of the Agriculture Committee.
No committee reported the bill, no floor vote was scheduled, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without further action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meat and poultry processors are better off: they avoided new OSHA standards, line-speed limits, attendance-policy rules, a private right of action for workers, and new Packers and Stockyards restrictions. Meat and poultry workers remain under the pre-existing, weaker safety and enforcement rules.

for.name: Rep. Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 2, 2023 and led it as sponsor.

for.name: 29 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 29 cosponsors were House Democrats.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or committee vote on the bill after it was referred to the committee and its Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry Subcommittee.

against.name: House leadership of the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: The multi-committee referral never resulted in a rule or floor consideration; no vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored and no committee or floor action ever occurred in the Republican-controlled House.

industries.note: The bill caps line-speed increases, adds OSHA standards and inspections, exposes them to worker lawsuits for retaliation, and restricts packer livestock ownership and contract practices. Their gain from the bill's defeat is workers' continued exposure to high injury rates in a highly concentrated industry.

industries.industry: Contract poultry growers and livestock ranchers
industries.note: The bill adds Packers and Stockyards Act remedies for growers and ranchers, restricts the poultry tournament pay system and certain forward contracts, and bars certain packer livestock ownership. These producers generally lack bargaining power against a small number of dominant buyers.
An additional $100 million in processing grants would expand small-plant capacity, and grant recipients could not sell to large packers for 10 years, supporting local competition.
Country-of-origin labeling for beef, pork, and dairy would impose labeling and supply-chain tracking costs, but gives shoppers origin information.

Grant eligibility requires labor peace agreements that give unions workplace access and card-check recognition if a majority of workers choose them, and the bill's safety and retaliation protections strengthen organizing conditions.
